**Solution 3 is the only candidate with a verified counterexample, so I take its answer, 9, as correct, with moderate confidence in the upper bound.**

**Lower bound (n₀ ≥ 9): SQS(8) fails at n = 8.** The Steiner quadruple system on 8 points (the 14 planes of AG(3,2)) is a {4}-graph in which every triple lies in exactly one block, so δ₃ = 1. Take any 5-set F. Its complement is a 3-set T, and inclusion–exclusion gives exactly 14 − 13 = 1 block disjoint from T, so F contains exactly one block B, with F = B ∪ {w}. In any cyclic ordering of F, the three consecutive triples containing w each have a private block outside F, which is fine. The two consecutive triples avoiding w lie inside B, and each of those triples is covered only by B. Two distinct edges are therefore needed from a single edge, so no Berge-C₅³ exists. The statement fails at t = 5 when n = 8.

**Upper bound (all n ≥ 9 work): not verified.** Solution 3's justification for n ≥ 9 is a sketch, and I did not check it fully. The obstructions I examined (uniquely covered triples, SQS-type structures) do not extend to larger n: for SQS(10), a 5-set containing no block exists, which gives a C₅ there, and 3-edges only add flexibility. I found no counterexample at n ≥ 9, but I did not rule one out exhaustively.

Solution 1 (7) and Solution 2 (6) are contradicted by the SQS(8) counterexample, which shows the property fails at n = 8.

CHOICE: 3
